name: Primavera De Filippi, Will Papper, Adrien Guerrera & Jake Hartnell, Aminals (GLITCH)
why: Fully on-chain lifeforms that feed on cryptocurrency and evolve as new SVG genes are added to their code; listed by the GLITCH collective. Launch date and who may add genes not verified; aminals.xyz is now a parked domain.

name: Scores for Meeting Otherwise, ed. Aio Frei, Franziska Koch and Irene Revell (Silver Press, November 2026)
why: Feminist history of the performance score from Pauline Oliveros onward, with newly commissioned scores; not yet published on 17 October 2026.

name: Tommy Hartung, The Old Testament (Snark.art)
why: Feature-length video in 25 chapters sold separately, 'intended for collective ownership' and reassemblable on the blockchain; check whether playing it whole requires owners to lend chapters as in 89 Seconds Atomized, and find the year.

name: World Computer Sculpture Garden contracts still without images: Echoes (0xhaiku), Dear God, Layer of Roads (Travelers) (Figure31), Yesbot (Sarah Friend), Critique of This Show (Rhea Myers et al.)
why: Participatory contracts in the 2024 contract show (visitors add words from a fixed dictionary, travel on Figure31's road, toggle Is Art via Yesbot, post critiques); all pass the test, but their sites render by script and no still image or video was found.

name: Agnieszka Kurant, The End of Signature (2015) and other crowd-sourced works
why: Kurant collects signatures from many people and merges them into one collective signature, and builds works from crowd data; check which works let a crowd produce the piece under her rules.

name: Brian Droitcour, 'Beautiful Rules' (Outland, 25 November 2025)
why: Essay arguing that Harm van den Dorpel fuses protocol and form so protocols can be judged as art; 2025, so outside the 2026 theory scope of pass4-leads-misc.

name: Blast Theory, Rider Spoke (2007) and A Machine To See With (2010)
why: Further Blast Theory works in which the public leaves recordings for later riders or follows phone instructions; check whether players' actions shape the work for others.

name: Figure31 & 0xfff, dear god, layer of roads (travelers) (2024)
why: Holders 'travel' forward or backward through Ethereum blocks; each journey adds to a shared landscape and leaves a monument sized to its length. Made for World Computer Sculpture Garden (contract 0x8170e7DB1AB0930D6afbBB67b7be81Dbd66B7c01). Passes the test; needs an image (the artist's S3 host blocks hotlinking, travelers.figure31.com is a JS app).

name: Figure31, MARK (2022)
why: 500 pre-minted fingerprint tokens on (GALLERY): the exhibition page emptied as collectors took pieces, ending as a blank screen (after Klein's The Void); sets of five unlock engraved silver rings. Check whether this counts as a collective protocol.

name: Leander Herzog, Likes (2026)
why: A single on-chain like button (Ethereum contract 0xE8A21c062352Bf135971410054Ef6c4D85Fa7bEc): anyone can like or unlike, and the count and list of likers are the work (93 likes on 13 Nov 2026). Needs a launch date, the artist's statement and an image.

name: James Bloom, GOLD (Fingerprints DAO, 2023)
why: 500-piece dynamic series whose images change in response to the collection's own live market activity; older onchain work, not yet checked in detail.

name: misha de ridder, glitch (Assembly)
why: 50 animated GIF tokens that degrade each time they are traded; check year, contract and whether degradation is enforced on-chain.

name: Agnes Cameron, Ed Fornieles, Manus Nijhoff & Jacob Willemsma, Sentences (2023)
why: On-chain sandbox for collaborative, prompt-based lore generation (cited in Le Random's 'Postgenerative Language Games').

name: Arb & 0xhank, Network States (2024)
why: On-chain strategy game in which LLMs generate lore from players' actions (cited in Le Random's 'Postgenerative Language Games'); check whether it is an art work.

name: dmstfctn, Godmode Epochs (2023–24)
why: Multiplayer AI-training clicker game (Serpentine, Alan Turing Institute; S+T+ARTS nomination); players' data later inscribed on-chain for Fango 1000. Non-chain participatory game; for the participatory batch.

name: Ivona Tau, 11:05 participatory video project (2026)
why: Collects anonymous short texts about what people were doing at 11:05 on a given day and uses them as prompts to steer her video archive; non-chain, for the participatory batch.

name: Ed Fornieles Studios, OMSK Social Club & Nina Runa Essendrop, The Group; A Temporary Autonomous Hotel (Athens Biennale, 2018)
why: Larp at Esperia Palace, 9–10 November 2018: visitors collect an identity and a room key at reception and must play their role inside rooms named for psychological positions. Only one image found so far.

name: Ed Fornieles, Dorm Daze (Facebook role-play performance)
why: Large-scale online performance in which participants took on Facebook profiles of American college students; date and documentation to verify.

name: Christian Falsnaes: Rise (2014), A Good Reason Is One That Looks Like One (2015), Stage (2017), Feast (2021)
why: Further audience-instruction works on the artist's site (instructions by microphone, loudspeaker or headphones); add if a later pass wants the artist's full set.

name: Shin Hanagata, CHIMERIA (Prix Ars Electronica 2026 Award of Distinction)
why: Five volunteers lived for two weeks in a Tokyo house with the eye moved to another part of the body by camera and headset, inventing new routines; performances let visitors enter. Check whether the artist's rules for the volunteers make it a group protocol.
